extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and editing of wartime news items for a general newspaper audience, including datelined dispatches, on-scene first-person accounts, military communiqués, human-interest pieces, and legal/political developments. Emphasizes attribution, censorship notes, timeliness labels, and use of official sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories explicitly attribute information to specific agencies, officials, correspondents or communiqués (e.g., 'By the Associated Press', 'the communique said', 'the Army announced', 'reported by the Berlin radio').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always identify the origin of factual claims and quotations (news agency, correspondent, official communique or radio broadcast). Use clear verbs such as 'said', 'reported', 'announced', and include dateline/correspondent byline where applicable to show provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship/compliance note
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain dispatches note editorial constraints: 'This story ... was received today from London after passing British censorship, but the exact date of the convoy battle was not disclosed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When material has been subject to governmental or military censorship, explicitly state that fact and identify any withheld details (for example, exact dates or locations). Flag to readers when censorship has potentially limited detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline and delay labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports include datelines and delay markers (examples: 'Ankara, April 20 (Delayed)', 'India, April 22 (P)', 'Canberra, April 22').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise datelines and, when a dispatch is late or delayed, mark it clearly. Datelines inform readers of where/when information originated and help set expectations for timeliness and verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-scene / first-person reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: First-person and on-board accounts are used for vivid reporting: 'This story was written recently by Associated Press War Correspondent Henry B. Jameson while aboard the Commodore’s ship...' and bylines like 'By LT. THOMAS HARMON...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label on-scene or eyewitness pieces with byline/location; include descriptive detail and personal observation to increase credibility. Distinguish clearly between first-hand accounts and second-hand reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of official military communiqués
rubrics_metrics.description: Military developments are frequently reported via official communiqués: phrases such as 'the communique said', 'a British communique said', and detailed lists of attacks/results appear throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on and cite official communiqués for reporting military operations, but indicate scope and limitations of those releases. When possible, corroborate with additional sources or note when only the official communique is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautious/hedged language for unconfirmed reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Unverified or uncertain information is presented with hedges: 'it was indicated', 'it has been reported', 'perhaps were stationed', 'it is believed here that...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use qualifying language when reports are unconfirmed. Make clear distinctions between verified facts and reports or rumors, and avoid presenting speculation as established fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest detail and personal identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Profiles and human-interest items include personal details, family references and quotations (e.g., the Goldstein family, Lt. Harmon’s jungle ordeal, lists of freed prisoners with hometowns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include identifying details (names, rank, hometown, family statements, vivid anecdotes) to humanize broad events. Ensure accurate spelling and verification of personal data; obtain family quotes where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lists of named individuals and hometowns
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports name multiple individuals and their home towns/ranks (example: long list of men 'captured by Axis forces in Egypt last June' with cities and ranks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide full names, ranks and hometowns for lists of people (prisoners, casualties, rescued). This aids identification and follow-up; verify spellings and permissions where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and multi-perspective sourcing on legal/political items
rubrics_metrics.description: Political/legal stories present multiple viewpoints and possible consequences (example: court ruling invalidating India Defense Rule and the comment that the Viceroy 'could issue an ordinance' to 'put the matter right').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When covering legal or political rulings, include the ruling, reactions from officials/experts, and discussion of likely next steps. Present differing viewpoints and legal context to help readers understand implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quoting military leaders and reporting assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: Commanders’ assessments and quoted judgments are used as authoritative evaluation (example: Gen. Harmon: 'we will stick to our plan of taking every opportunity to strike the most vulnerable targets' and 'the Jap is perhaps about 60 per cent as efficient as our pilots').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote high-ranking officers and officials for strategic assessments, but note the scope and subjectivity of their statements. Contextualize quoted percentages or evaluations and, where possible, provide corroborating operational data or alternative analyses.
